item.title: China to boost new types of energy storage during 2026-2030
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 09:01:00
CHINA / SOCIETY China to boost new types of energy storage during 2026-2030 By Xinhua Published: Nov 14, 2026 09:01 AM
China will accelerate the development of new types of energy storage during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) to support the building of a new electric power system, according to a plan released on Friday. The plan, issued by the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration (NEA), sets a target of 300 million kilowatts of installed new types of energy storage by 2030, with an average storage duration of about three hours. It also aims to shift the sector from large-scale expansion to market-driven growth. New types of energy storage refer to energy storage technologies other than pumped-storage hydropower, mainly including electrochemical, compressed-air and gravity storage. The plan calls for new types of energy storage to participate fairly in electricity markets, and encourages renewable energy megabases equipped with storage to join cross-provincial power markets as a single entity. It also calls for a refined pricing mechanism that reflects the value of stored power, with charging and discharging prices set through fair market trading. The emphasis on market mechanisms comes as China's power market increasingly matures. Investment in new types of energy storage was initially policy-driven, relying largely on mandatory deployment rules and subsidies, but the sector is now shifting toward market-based mechanisms, Huayuan Securities said in a research report. Xu Dongjie, deputy chief engineer of the China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute, called the 300-million-kilowatt target a prudent, science-based minimum target that meets system needs and supports a reasonable rise in utilization while giving the industry confidence and preventing investment-driven boom-and-bust cycles. China leads the world in new types of energy storage, with installed capacity accounting for around 40 percent of the global total. By the end of 2025, China had built and put into operation 136 million kilowatts of new types of energy storage, with average storage duration reaching 2.58 hours, 0.3 hours longer than at the end of 2024, according to the NEA.

item.title: Eurocontrol suspends US-bound flight departures from member states
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 08:59:00
WORLD / AMERICAS Eurocontrol suspends US-bound flight departures from member states By Xinhua Published: Nov 14, 2026 08:59 AM
Eurocontrol said on Friday that all flights departing from its member states for U.S. airports were suspended at the request of the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration due to technical issues. The suspension covers departures between 2200 GMT on Friday and 0500 GMT on Saturday, the European air traffic management agency said in a notice posted at 2303 GMT. Eurocontrol's Network Manager Operations Center in Brussels said it was closely monitoring the situation and would provide updates. Eurocontrol is an intergovernmental organization with 42 member states, including Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Türkiye, that supports air traffic management across Europe.

item.title: Mutual growth of foreign firms, Chinese market is setting an example for openness in the Asia-Pacific: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 00:35:00
Lujiazui Photo:VCG In recent days, new developments of two long-established multinational corporations in the Chinese market have drawn the attention of Bloomberg, Reuters and other international media outlets. In October, German car brand Volkswagen saw its new-energy vehicle (NEV) deliveries in China surge by nearly 350 percent year-on-year, exceeding 28,000 units - a new monthly record. Meanwhile, US financial firm Citigroup views Chinese enterprises "going global" as a significant growth opportunity, with its China-related business posting double-digit growth for many consecutive years. For this manufacturing giant and this Wall Street bank, what they gained in China are more than just orders, but greater capabilities. While it was once common to hear that foreign firms viewed China merely as a "contract manufacturing hub," they now prefer to view the country as a vibrant "innovation workshop" - an environment where companies from diverse backgrounds engage in healthy competition and mutual learning, driving both technological iteration and the enhancement of global competitiveness. As one of the first multinational corporations to enter the Chinese market, Volkswagen must have gained a profound understanding of the unique value this market holds. Faced with a 30-percent decline in vehicle deliveries during the first three quarters of this year, the company chose to partner with XPeng to co-develop an all-new electronic and electrical architecture, collaborated with Horizon Robotics to address gaps in its intelligent driving capabilities, and established its largest R&D hub outside of Germany in Hefei. The intense competitive landscape and rapidly evolving consumer demands in China are compelling a century-old automotive giant like Volkswagen to continuously recalibrate its strategy and strengthen its core competencies, ensuring it avoids the risk of "atrophy" in the face of global competition. More importantly, the significance of the Chinese market for corporate development has long transcended the notion of a mere "fitness regimen." An increasing number of multinational corporations have completed a comprehensive evolution in China, ranging from technical adaptation and trial-and-error experimentation with business models to the complete restructuring of their operational systems. The new products, technologies, and business models refined here have not only enabled these firms to secure a firm foothold in China but have also been exported to global markets, granting them a distinct, competitive edge on the international stage. This transition from simply "benefiting in China" to "growing up in China" represents one of the most vivid new opportunities that the process of Chinese modernization offers to the global economy. This phenomenon, where a company coexists and co-develops with the market, is an inevitable outcome of the ongoing evolution of the Chinese innovation ecosystem. Take Volkswagen's transformation as an example: through partnerships with local firms, the company has become deeply embedded in the innovation network of China's NEV industry, rapidly addressing its own capability gaps for the era of intelligent mobility. The mature, refined technical solutions developed here are now being considered to upgrade vehicle models back in Europe. There are many more similar stories: Adient has rolled out product plans developed in its Chongqing R&D center to its 180 manufacturing sites worldwide, while Siemens Healthineers has exported over 150 products manufactured locally in China to more than 150 countries and regions. "What is learned in China is being monetized globally" - this has become a shared consensus among multinational corporate executives in their private discussions. Even more noteworthy is that a number of service-oriented multinational corporations are upgrading their own operational capabilities as they follow the global expansion of Chinese industries. Citigroup's strategic shift serves as a prime example: While foreign banks previously entered China primarily to serve multinational firms expanding into the Chinese market, they must now grasp the global strategic logic of Chinese new-energy enterprises, navigate the financial flow regulations of cross-border e-commerce, and tailor their services to the localized operational needs of Chinese companies in emerging markets. These capabilities, honed within the Chinese market, have, in turn, become unique advantages that allow these institutions to broaden their service reach on a global scale. This two-way empowerment has moved beyond the traditional, one-way flow of expertise from foreign firms to China, fostering a new landscape where Chinese and foreign enterprises learn from and support one another as they jointly explore global markets. Viewed through the lens of the 2026 APEC meeting in Shenzhen, the symbiotic practices currently unfolding in the Chinese market serve as a compelling illustration of the three key priorities championed by this year's APEC: openness, innovation, and cooperation. Industrial interaction within the Chinese market has transcended traditional frameworks; market participants from diverse backgrounds no longer function merely as isolated links in a supply chain. Instead, they engage in deep collaboration within an open innovation ecosystem - learning from one another through robust competition, jointly refining new technologies and business models, and ultimately cultivating fresh, globally-oriented competitiveness. This pragmatic experience, forged within the Chinese market, offers a tangible, actionable model for the Asia-Pacific region as it seeks to dismantle technical barriers, strengthen industrial chain resilience, and achieve more inclusive, shared prosperity. Today's global economy remains overshadowed by geopolitical conflicts, rising protectionism, and lackluster growth momentum. Many are anxious about the rhetoric surrounding "decoupling" and "severing supply chains" and concerned about the fragmentation of global markets. As a pivotal pole in the global economic landscape characterized by both substantial scale and a dynamic capacity for innovation, China neither forms exclusive, closed-off circles nor seeks a "winner-takes-all" unipolar advantage. Instead, through the continuous opening of its market and its commitment to innovation-driven development, China provides a platform for enterprises from all nations to grow together. As successive waves of multinational corporations return to the global marketplace, armed with new capabilities honed in China, they bring with them not only more efficient technologies and business models, but also a fundamental development philosophy that openness fosters progress, and cooperation catalyzes innovation. This represents the long-term value that the Chinese market contributes to the global economy - a value that transcends short-term gains.

item.title: Peru sees APEC, upgraded China FTA as drivers of investment cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14 00:26:00
Carlos Vásquez Corrales, Peruvian ambassador to China, gives a keynote speech in Beijing on November 13, 2026. Photo: Dong Feng/Global Times Peru is looking to move beyond its traditional focus on mining, energy and infrastructure cooperation with China and attract more investment in manufacturing and other value-added industries, the country's ambassador to China said on Friday, as the Peruvian Embassy in Beijing launched an investment guide for Chinese businesses. The report, titled Peru's Investment Climate Assessment Report - a guide for Chinese investors, is designed to provide Chinese companies with information to support investment decisions and deepen economic cooperation between the two countries. Carlos Vásquez Corrales, Peruvian ambassador to China, described the report as a practical tool for supporting the next stage of bilateral economic relations. He said China is Peru's largest trading partner and one of its most important sources of foreign investment. The two countries should ensure that international trade and foreign investment contribute not only to economic growth, but also to productivity, employment, innovation and greater participation in global value chains, Vásquez said. A key priority for Peru is to transform its role in the economic relationship with China, moving from primarily serving as a logistics link between South America and Asia to becoming a platform for production, manufacturing and value-added exports. The Port of Chancay, a major infrastructure project developed with Chinese participation, has significantly improved maritime connectivity between South America and Asia, Vásquez said. However, he noted that connectivity should be followed by greater productive capacity. The launch comes as China prepares to host the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19. Speaking to the Global Times, the ambassador also highlighted the role of APEC as a platform for bilateral exchanges between leaders. He pointed to the upgraded protocol to the China-Peru Free Trade Agreement (FTA), signed in 2024 in the presence of the two countries' leaders and which took effect on November 1, 2026. The upgraded agreement includes new provisions on e-commerce and global supply chains, among other areas. Vásquez said these provisions could help Peruvian micro, small and medium-sized enterprises gain access to Chinese and wider Asia-Pacific markets, while integrating into industrial chains for electric vehicles and electronic components. He said the Chancay Port project and the upgraded FTA together provide a model of connectivity linking Latin America with the Asia-Pacific region. Cooperation under the APEC framework, he added, can further strengthen South-South cooperation and bring tangible benefits to people across Latin America. China and Peru are both members of the Global South and share common positions on multilateral platforms such as APEC, Shi Zhiqin, a professor at Tsinghua University's Institute of the Belt and Road Initiative, said at the event, adding that their cooperation in supporting multilateralism and South-South cooperation could serve as an example for other countries.

item.title: With less than a week left, AI assistants, multilingual translation terminals and driverless shuttles appear in Shenzhen to greet visitors
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 23:59:00
A humanoid robot greets visitors at a coffee kiosk in Shenzhen on October 11, 2026. Photo: VCG The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province, on November 18-19. With less than a week to go before the meeting opens, the city has entered what it calls "APEC time," as preparations are in full swing. From AI-powered airport services and autonomous driving to next-generation communications networks, Shenzhen is set to showcase how technological innovation is reshaping urban life and facilitating international exchanges. As a key transportation hub in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport will serve as the first stop for many APEC delegates arriving in the city. In preparation for the event, the airport has launched a new AI-powered travel assistant, an intelligent agent capable of interacting with passengers in multiple languages and providing real-time answers to questions about entry procedures, transportation connections and other travel-related matters. Multilingual AI translation terminals have also been installed at the ground transportation center's information desk and the service center for international passengers, supporting real-time translation in 38 languages. The airport is also accelerating the development of smart services, including an international facial recognition boarding system. Incoming passengers can submit their entry information in advance using electronic QR codes. During immigration clearance, a dual-screen, dual-camera information collection device can complete the collection of passenger information in as little as one minute, further improving clearance efficiency. At an autonomous driving bus shelter near Luohu Port, Shenzhen's Level 4 autonomous driving route, the first to operate in a bustling downtown area, is offering another glimpse of the city's smart mobility ambitions. The minibuses are equipped with more than 20 sensors, including LiDAR and cameras, enabling 360-degree environmental perception and autonomous obstacle avoidance. Large central control screens inside the vehicles display real-time road conditions in digital form, according to the China National Radio (CNR). Self-driving vehicles are now available in multiple districts across Shenzhen. Passengers can unlock the vehicles with a passcode, while the vehicles can independently recognize traffic lights, change lanes and navigate complex intersections. An in-car AI assistant can also respond to voice commands, allowing passengers to choose music to listen to, activate a massage chair or change the temperature. Communications infrastructure is also being upgraded to support the international event. At transportation hubs and border checkpoints, the deployment of ultra-high-bandwidth coordinated networking technology is designed to ensure uninterrupted connectivity as users move across different areas. Field tests have recorded peak downlink speeds of 1.5 gigabits per second, while maintaining stable speeds of 10 megabits per second even during peak periods involving tens of thousands of users. The technology has significantly improved network performance in high-density environments. Modern Diplomacy, an online platform covering international affairs, noted that Shenzhen was chosen to host this year's APEC meeting particularly given its reputation as China's Silicon Valley and a global hub for AI and embodied intelligence. The city will showcase its advanced industrial ecosystem in robotics, new vehicles, and the digital economy, aiming to connect markets and economies across the Asia-Pacific region. In the first three quarters of this year, Shenzhen's value-added output in high-tech manufacturing increased by 11.6 percent year-on-year, while that of advanced manufacturing rose by 11.9 percent. Output of major high-tech products also maintained rapid growth. Production of 3D printing equipment, industrial robots and lithium-ion batteries increased by 77.8 percent, 44.1 percent and 38.5 percent, respectively, according to data released by the Shenzhen municipal statistics bureau on October 23. item.title: Wuhan school introduces screen-free tutoring, pupils found more focused in classes
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 23:51:00
Students at Wuhan Optics Valley International School attended classes without watching any screens on November 11 in Wuhan, Central China's Hubei Province. Students at Wuhan Optics Valley International School attended classes without watching any screens on November 11 in Wuhan, Central China's Hubei Province, and they followed the teachers' gestures and narrations closely. This is the second month the school has held screen-free classes for an entire day. Since September 1, the school has let six grades take turns to have one day with no power points projected onto screens. Students had to learn face-to-face, using only their books, the blackboard, and other printed materials. Zhai Xiaomeng, a teacher for the fourth grade, prepared her classes using an interactive approach. Zhai was quoted as saying that power points were more colorful and students had got used to them, but since the screen-free day was introduced, she decided to slow down the tutoring rhythm and arranged writing ideas on the blackboard. Students had more opportunities to think over story plots by discussing them in teams, and Zhai was able to capture their learning feedback in a timely manner. "In a classroom without electronic screens, I can concentrate well by looking at the teacher and the blackboard," said Tian Yixin, a student at the school. One of the staff members in charge of the campaign said that the aims of the screen-free day were to protect students' eyesight, reduce the strain of prolonged screen time, encourage teachers to think out of the box in terms of their teaching approaches and to help students get more focused on learning and thinking. "After two months of implementing the 'Eye Protection Screen-Off Day,' we have found that students' concentration in class has improved, and they have developed the habit of thinking calmly and independently. Teachers' blackboard writing and lesson design abilities have greatly improved, and there has been an increase in in-depth face-to-face interaction between teachers and students," the staff member said. item.description:

Photo: VCG China strictly prohibits all forms of surrogacy, and organizing surrogacy constitutes a criminal offense, violates ethical norms, and will be subject to severe legal penalties, National Health Commission spokesperson Yang Jinrui said on Friday. So-called "surrogacy agreements" are not protected by law, and those involved may also be held legally accountable, according to the spokesperson. Some localities in China have reported cases involving surrogacy or the alleged illegal use of assisted reproductive technologies. For example, CCTV News reported that health and public security authorities in Changsha, Central China's Hunan Province, raided two underground facilities illegally providing assisted reproductive services in the city's Yuelu district on October 29, detaining 21 people suspected of involvement in illegal surrogacy and seizing drugs and medical equipment. item.title: It's Jensen Huang today. Who is next? Washington's list of targets may keep growing
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 11:33:00
Nvidia's co-founder Jensen Huang Photo: VCG Jensen Huang, one of the most prominent figures in the global AI boom, has resigned. The immediate trigger, as presented in public, was a series of reports about his private life. But from the initial reports in the New York Times to the intense coverage across US media, the controversy has become about far more than a personal matter. Huang's affair was framed from the outset as a matter of US national security. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote in an X post, "Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." This is a pattern worth watching closely amid the current US climate of technological competition with China. First, an individual case is used to ignite public debate; then the framework of "national security" is invoked to elevate it into an issue of systemic risk. In today's Washington, "national security" can sometimes be invoked without reference to a concrete, verifiable threat, becoming a narrative tool that can be applied to prominent ethnic Chinese professionals operating at the intersection of US-China tech competition. The Huang case illustrates this pattern starkly: he lobbied for chip exports to China - a move that could be portrayed as potentially endangering national security; he reportedly had a personal relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence of having ties to Chinese intelligence - another "potential national security concern;" and he wielded influence in Washington while maintaining business ties with China - again, grounds for raising "national security concerns." The word "may" is the key. It allows suspicion to be cast without establishing that wrongdoing has occurred or reaching a verdict. In this climate, a combination of Chinese identity and political circumstances can be enough to turn a celebrated business leader into a perceived security risk. The more accomplished and influential a person is, and the more centrally positioned they are between China and the US, the more vulnerable they may become to being singled out in the name of "national security." More alarming is the way this is reinforced by a broader narrative that demonizes China. China is cast as a strategic competitor of the US, while "national security precautions" imposed on the entire Chinese community are being heightened to an unprecedented degree. "The Jensen Huang affair exposes corporate America's China problem" - read a headline by The Hill. But this problem was not created by China; it reflects a contradiction within the US itself. On one hand, the US relies on the creativity and expertise of top Chinese talent; on the other, it increasingly treats them as potential security threats. It needs Nvidia's technology and global competitiveness, yet it does not want the company to make its own commercial decisions about the Chinese market. That is the real contradiction. This contradiction will not stop with Jensen Huang alone. The next target could well be other tech entrepreneurs unwilling to fully align with Washington's political agenda - including those who might argue that the US should win by running faster rather than by tripping up its opponents. In the current US political environment, ordinary business logic has come to be seen as "politically incorrect." Entrepreneurs are being forced to fight on two fronts at once: the technology race in the global market, and political scrutiny in Washington. Many in Silicon Valley will probably have to weigh every decision carefully: asking not whether they have done anything wrong, but whether their business decisions involving China and the US might one day be recast as "national security risks." It's Jensen Huang today. Who is next? Perhaps Washington is already looking for the answer.

item.title: Why becoming a 'gatekeeper' for US protectionism is not in Mexico's interest
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13 00:27:00
US Mexico Illustration: Xia Qing/GT Washington has erected a wall of protectionism around the globe, and Mexico is eager to pass it more bricks, helping plug the "loopholes." But the higher this wall rises, the more likely it is to hem in Mexico itself, constraining not only its development prospects but also its independence in shaping trade policy. According to Reuters, Luis Rosendo Gutierrez, Mexico's deputy economy minister for foreign trade, said on Wednesday that the Mexican government had tightened traceability measures with industry to ensure that no steel from China or other countries is rerouted through its territory into the US by exploiting Mexico's trade preferences. Meanwhile, Mexico is urging Washington to ease tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and automobiles. Jiang Shixue, a distinguished professor at Hangzhou Normal University, told the Global Times that Mexico's move is rooted in its economic predicament created by strong dependence on the US. Facing US tariff pressure and uncertainty surrounding the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement review, Mexico hopes that aligning itself with Washington's restrictions on trade with China will win concessions from the US. Since 2025, Mexico has repeatedly followed the US to announce measures to impose tariffs on imports from China and other countries without free-trade agreements. It seems that Mexico is actively standing guard at the door on Washington's behalf. While other countries may justify trade barriers as necessary to protect their own industries, Mexico's restrictions appear to be protecting the interests of a "third party." In effect, Mexico risks turning itself into a gatekeeper for Washington's protectionism. This could end up as a potential "Faustian bargain." Mexico hopes to sacrifice part of its economic and trade cooperation with China in exchange for US concessions on tariffs and trade. But it may discover that what it surrenders far outweighs what it could gain. On the one hand, Washington is unlikely to abandon its trade pressure on Mexico. On the other, Mexico risks sacrificing long-term industrial cooperation, supply chain diversification and, ultimately, its economic sovereignty. According to Gutierrez, the country has already reduced steel and aluminum imports from countries including China, South Korea and India, by about 30 percent. Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, pointed out that manufacturing is a pillar of Mexico's economy, and steel and aluminum are essential inputs for industries such as auto manufacturing and machinery. Cutting imports of these materials could further aggravate supply pressures on Mexican manufacturers, disrupting production and undermining supply chain stability. More importantly, if Mexico can readily change its trade policies under external pressure, other countries may begin to question the stability and predictability of its investment and trade environment, he added. Once policy predictability is undermined, the price Mexico pays could go far beyond the immediate costs of tariffs. Just one day before the report, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum stressed that respect for sovereignty and cooperation free from subordination "are non-negotiable" tenets of Mexico's relations with the US. True sovereignty should not be confined to political rhetoric. It should be reflected in a country's ability to independently choose its trading partners, allocate resources according to its development needs and formulate its own economic and trade policies. In an increasingly interconnected global economy, broader international partnerships give countries greater room to maneuver amid external uncertainties. Canada, also deeply integrated into the North American economic system, has not abandoned efforts to diversify its trading partners and is actively seeking to expand cooperation with China and other economies to get rid of its dependence on the US. America's trade wall is America's choice. Mexico has no reason to turn it into its own barrier to development. What Mexico truly needs is not to become another brick in Washington's protectionist wall, but to safeguard its economic sovereignty, preserve its ability to connect with global markets and participate in international industrial chains. Otherwise, in trying to please Washington, Mexico risks cutting off its nose to spite its face.

item.title: Dancing to their own beat
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-12 23:38:00
Members of a rural women's dance group perform in Linzhou, Central China's Henan Province, on March 6, 2026. The group, which has been getting a lot of attention online, gathers almost every afternoon to livestream their dance performances. Photo: VCG What do older people in rural areas do with their days? Work the fields, look after grandchildren or simply sit in the sun and reminisce? In a courtyard in Linzhou, Central China's Henan Province, a lively beat fills the air. A group of rural women averaging around 55 years of age stretch and sway with bright smiles as they livestream themselves dancing, attracting thousands of viewers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. Farm work and housework chores fill their days; dancing on livestream offers a fleeting respite that belongs to them alone. This once-niche form of rural livestreaming has become more than just an online sensation. It is an attempt by older people to reclaim a sense of self and a vivid reflection of the changing cultural life in rural China. Another way to live Nearly 60-year-old Jiao Jianyu is the dance group's front-and-center performer. During live streams, she often appears in red, dancing with unmatched fervor, and is frequently singled out by online viewers as the group's standout performer. "Jiao is a natural-born dancer. She can pick up a dance after watching it just once or twice, and there's natural spark and energy in her movements," Chen Hongyu, founder of the rural woman dancing group, told the Global Times. Off camera, however, Jiao's life is very different. Her husband works as a migrant laborer in the city, leaving her to shoulder the burden of farm work and care for elderly family members and children at home. Her 35-year-old son has an intellectual disability and a cognitive development level comparable to that of a three-year-old, requiring constant care to keep him safe. It was only after a fan asked if something was troubling her that she began making a conscious effort to smile and appear more cheerful on camera. Since then, fans have cheered her on, with her infectious laughter filling the air. That kind of encouragement, she told the Global Times, is like warm sunshine, easing the hardships of daily life and giving her "fresh motivation to carry on." Jiao also helps organize the dancers' formations and decide the order of performances during livestreams. She knows the entire dance routine and has a keen eye for the personalities and strengths of local women hoping to join the group. "Those in the front row need to have good memories, since everyone behind follows their lead. Those with a knack for humor help liven things up and draw viewers in," she said shyly. Asked how livestream dancing had changed her life the most, she said, "These broadcasts give me a change of scenery, allowing me to break free from the tedious, unrelenting routine of housework." Jiao is not alone in finding a new sense of purpose through dancing. Zhang Ruifang, who is always seen smiling on camera, lost her son late last year. He had loved dancing and, before he passed away, encouraged his mother to do what she loved. His encouragement prompted Zhang to take up dancing, helping her cope with her grief. Jiao recalled Zhang telling the group that dancing made her feel as though her son were still by her side, with every step bringing back memories of him. Li Ying, 55, has also found solace through the group. For years, her mother, who has Alzheimer's disease, required round-the-clock care, leaving Li largely housebound. That changed once the livestreams started. Now she brings her mother along to the dance sessions. The older woman seems to enjoy the lively atmosphere, and her mood has noticeably brightened. For Li, the change has brought some much-needed relief after years of caregiving. "Life has dealt me its hardships and burdens, yet I refuse to wallow in self-pity. Life is not just about getting by. It's about finding joy," Li said. Chen explained that most of these women, facing age-related and other barriers, struggle to find work outside the village. Meanwhile, cultural and recreational activities in the village are few and far between. "When we first started the livestreams, we simply wanted to give them something to do and let them see that there is another way to live," he said. Bright glow Now, 40 to 50 older women take part in the livestreams each day. This informal dance group has attracted more than 270,000 followers on Douyin, with its livestreams regularly drawing thousands of concurrent viewers. The women earn roughly 50 yuan ($7.50) a day through livestreaming. For them, that modest income means more than just money. "Dancing gives me something to look forward to every day, and I can also earn a little extra to help with household expenses," Jiao said. "It makes me feel that even at my age, I can still realize my own potential." The props they use add a homespun charm. Lion heads, colored balls and wooden horses are all handmade by the women themselves, reworked from discarded materials. The approach keeps costs down, but it also weaves local creativity into every performance, turning the props into a highlight of the livestream room. Although their dance moves lack professional polish and their choreography is simple, the women's unpretentious charm has struck a chord with many netizens. "They don't strive for perfection, they simply enjoy dancing. There's a warmth in their everyday lives that reminds me how ordinary people can make even the simplest lives shine," one netizen wrote. Jia Zhiwen, head of the village's Party committee, said livestreams have brought the village greater online visibility, while also challenging traditional stereotypes of rural women and enriching their spiritual lives during the agricultural off-season. As for the future, the troupe members have no grand plans. "Holding hope for tomorrow is the best plan of all," Jiao said.
